About this citation

The Analects is a compiled record of sayings, not a work by Confucius. The common formula 'Confucius said' refers to a tradent whose words were assembled by later hands, and the book-and-chapter locator is what makes a passage findable in any edition.

### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“The Master said: If one hears the Way in the morning, one may die content that evening.”

Classical Chinese

“朝聞道，夕死可矣。”

Literally: “In the morning hear the Way; at evening die — acceptable.” Eight characters, no subject. The English “one may die content” supplies a subject and an emotional state that the Chinese leaves to the reader.

#### Forms in circulation that differ

-   “If one hears the Way in the morning, one may die content that evening.”
-   “If a man in the morning hears the truth, he may die in the evening without regret.”

### Attribution notes

Analects 4.8. The character 道 is rendered “the Way” here and “the truth” in several nineteenth-century translations — including the one that circulated most widely — and the two choices are not equivalent: 道 in the Analects is a course of conduct and a tradition, not a proposition that can be true. Readers searching the “truth” wording are usually looking at James Legge's rendering without knowing it.

#### About Confucius

Confucius (Kong Qiu, 551–479 BCE) taught in the late Spring and Autumn period amid the Zhou order’s political fragmentation. Born in the state of Lu, he briefly held local office and then spent years seeking rulers who would adopt ritual-based, virtue-centered government.

### Interpretation

In the Analects the "Way" (dao) is not a doctrine but a pattern of right order that can be perceived in conduct, ritual, and governance. Confucius is not praising early death; he is ranking the objects of concern. If understanding the Way is what makes a life intelligible, then once it is genuinely heard, duration adds nothing comparable. The morning-evening construction makes the point by compressing time to nothing, so the listener cannot treat the claim as a trade to be calculated.

#### Why it matters

Read it as a question about attention rather than mortality: what would you need to understand for the rest of your life to feel complete rather than merely longer? Most people never name that thing, and so accumulate years without the sense of arrival.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “The Master said: If one hears the Way…”?

“The Master said: If one hears the Way…” comes from The Analects, 4.8 (c. 5th–3rd century BCE (compiled)), attributed to Confucius.

#### What does Confucius mean by inquiry?

Socratic elenchus, scientific method, and pragmatist experimentalism treat inquiry as self-correcting. The ethics of inquiry asks for intellectual honesty. This passage enters that discussion through inquiry, life.

#### Is the wording of this Confucius quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “The Master said: If one hears the Way in the morning, one may die content that evening.” Forms in circulation that differ: If one hears the Way in the morning, one may die content that evening. / If a man in the morning hears the truth, he may die in the evening without regret. The Classical Chinese reads “朝聞道，夕死可矣。”

#### Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Analects 4.8. The character 道 is rendered “the Way” here and “the truth” in several nineteenth-century translations — including the one that circulated most widely — and the two choices are not equivalent: 道 in the Analects is a course of conduct and a tradition, not a proposition that can be true. Readers searching the “truth” wording are usually looking at James Legge's rendering without knowing it.
